passage: The engagement party in Nitin's village had one bar of network, and only on the roof. Varun sat at home with his phone clutched to his chest. Four messages, no reply. His heart pounded as if someone were chasing him. He typed a fifth: "Are you there? Why are you ignoring me?" His thumb stopped above send. It felt like he would die if he didn't hear back. But some corner of his mind asked whether that was really love or whether it was fear, and he put the phone face down on the bed. He went to his elder brother Chirag, who was fixing a bicycle, and said, "I can't stop. I keep needing to check." Chirag handed him a spanner. "Talk to me. And maybe the counsellor at school." Varun held the wheel and breathed.

qa.q: Why did Varun have so little contact with Nitin that evening?
qa.a: The engagement party in Nitin's village had only one bar of network, and only on the roof.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he held the phone, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Panic. His heart pounded as if someone were chasing him, and it felt like he would die if he did not hear back.

qa.q: What did Varun do that was wise?
qa.a: He did not send the fifth message. He put the phone face down, told his brother Chirag what was happening and accepted the idea of seeing the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Nitin see the flood of messages?
qa.a: Nitin would probably feel crowded or pressured, especially while trying to enjoy a family party, so holding back protects them both.

grounding: Varun feels he will die without his partner and needs constant reassurance, recognises it as anxiety, does not monitor Nitin, and seeks support.

passage:
When I was with Vivek, I felt like I couldn't breathe without him. That's what I told myself was love.
I needed him to text me every hour. If he didn't reply in ten minutes, my heart pounded and I imagined he'd stopped caring. I asked him to share his location "just so I know you're okay." I checked who he'd followed. At night I'd ask, "Do you still love me?" three, four times.
One evening my older sister Sharmila found me crying over an unanswered message, curled up like a little girl. She sat with me and said gently, "Hansa, this sounds more like fear than love."
That word, fear, stuck. I went to the school counsellor that week. She helped me see it was anxiety, and that tracking Vivek wasn't care, it was control.
I stopped asking for his location. I joined the badminton club again. Some days are still hard. But I can breathe on my own now.

qa.q: How often did Hansa need Vivek to text?
What was Hansa feeling when Vivek didn't reply quickly?
qa.a: She felt panicky and afraid, her heart pounding as she imagined he had stopped caring.

qa.q: Which steps helped Hansa, and why?
qa.a: Listening to Sharmila, seeing the counsellor, stopping the location tracking and rejoining badminton helped her see the anxiety and build her own life.

qa.q: How might Vivek have felt about Hansa's constant check-ins?
qa.a: Vivek may have felt pressured and watched, as if he had to prove his love every hour.

grounding: A teen who needs constant reassurance from her partner realises it is anxiety rather than love, seeks support and builds her own interests.

passage:
Football coach's note, under-17 squad, Tuesday
Over the past month, Jeevan's focus in training has dropped. He checks his phone between every drill. Today he left the pitch twice to text, and when he came back he was pale.
His teammate Darshan told me Jeevan messages his girlfriend, Mitali, almost every few minutes, and gets upset if she doesn't reply straight away. Darshan said Jeevan once asked him to check who Mitali was chatting with in the canteen, and Darshan refused.
After training I sat with Jeevan on the bench. He admitted, "If I don't know where she is, I feel like I'm going to fall apart." I told him that sounds like anxiety, not love, and that watching her would hurt them both.
He agreed to see the school counsellor. I walked him to the counsellor's office before he went home today. I'll also give him back a leadership role in drills, so he has something of his own to focus on.

qa.q: What did Darshan refuse to do?
qa.a: To check who Mitali was chatting with in the canteen.

qa.q: How does Jeevan feel when he doesn't know where Mitali is?
qa.a: He feels anxious and panicky, as if he is going to fall apart.

qa.q: How did the coach support Jeevan wisely?
qa.a: By naming the feelings as anxiety not love, saying monitoring would hurt them both, walking him to the counsellor the same day and giving him a role of his own.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Jeevan's behaviour?
qa.a: Darshan seems worried and uncomfortable, refusing to help watch Mitali and telling the coach because he cares about Jeevan.

grounding: A coach observes a teen who needs constant check-ins from his girlfriend, names it as anxiety, and connects him with support.
